I'm auditing ATMOSPHERE and NARRATIVE TEXTURE in a top-down 3D LLM-NPC town game (C++ / raylib). I need an evidence-backed inventory of the world's authored content and ambient detail as it exists RIGHT NOW. Report facts only with file:line (or file path) evidence — no recommendations, just what's actually authored into the world.

Explore:
- personas/ directory (or wherever .persona files live) — read several fully. How many NPCs, how richly written, what personalities, do they reference each other or the town? What structured fields (schedule, position, backstory, knowledge)?
- The city/world layout code (city generation, building placement, plaza, zones) in src/core and src/app — is the town hand-authored or procedural? Are there named places, signage, districts with identity?
- Ambient life: crowds, pedestrians, cars/traffic — how many, do they have any character or are they anonymous movers?
- Any environmental storytelling: props placed to imply narrative, text/signs in world, anything that says a person lives here vs a grid of assets.
- Sound/music ambience (check quickly).
- The town's premise/setting: is there a stated fiction (what town, what era, why these people)? Check README, plans, persona content.

Answer concretely: (1) Does the world feel authored or assembled — what specific evidence each way? (2) How many named, characterized NPCs exist and how deep is each? (3) Is there any sense of PLACE (named locations, local identity) or is it a generic asset grid? (4) What ambient/environmental detail exists vs is absent? Cite files/lines.

# LLM NPC City

A small first-person 3D city where every inhabitant is a live LLM character.
Walk the streets, find the baker, the cop, the busker, the hot-dog vendor —
press `T` and talk to them about anything. Each NPC has their own personality,
their own knowledge of the city (and pointed ignorance of everything else),
and remembers your conversation.

Powered locally by [Ollama](https://ollama.com) — no cloud, no API key.

## Quick start (Windows)

1. **Install Ollama** from <https://ollama.com/download>, then pull the model:

   ```
   ollama pull qwen2.5:3b-instruct
   ```

2. **Install MSYS2** from <https://www.msys2.org> and, in the *UCRT64* shell:

   ```
   pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-cmake
   ```

3. **Fetch the art packs** (once): `bash tools/fetch_assets.sh` — two CC0
   low-poly packs, pinned and checksummed (see `assets/LICENSES.md`).

4. **Double-click `run.bat`** (or run `./run.ps1`). It checks Ollama is up,
   builds (CMake fetches raylib automatically), and launches the game.

## Playing

- `WASD` to walk, mouse to look around.
- Walk up to anyone: `[T] Talk to <name>` appears — press `T`.
- Type, press `Enter`, and watch the reply stream in live. `Escape` to leave.
- `Escape` opens the pause menu: resume, quit, or **rebind every key with the
  mouse** (changes save instantly).

Full reference: [docs/CONTROLS.md](docs/CONTROLS.md).

## Multiplayer (2-4 friends)

One player hosts; up to three more walk the same city and talk to the same
NPCs — one shared brain per character, so the baker remembers what your
friend told her.

**Hosting:** `Escape` → **Multiplayer** → **Host on port 40605**. Your machine
runs the world and the LLM; nobody else needs Ollama. Tell your friends your
IP address (`ipconfig` / `ifconfig`, e.g. `192.168.1.20`).

**Joining:** `Escape` → **Multiplayer** → click the address field, type
`<host-ip>:40605`, press `Enter`. Connection problems show up right there —
wrong address, full session (4 players max), or mismatched game versions.

What to expect in a session:

- Everyone sees everyone walk around, plus each NPC's live position and mood.
- NPC conversations are private to read, public in effect: if your friend
  angers Officer Brooks, you'll see her scowl.
- An NPC answers one person at a time; a second question waits its turn.
- Only the host's world persists — when the host quits, the session ends.

**Beyond your LAN:** the internet can't reach your living room uninvited.
Either forward TCP port 40605 on the host's router, or skip router config
entirely with [Tailscale](https://tailscale.com)/ZeroTier (both make a
private network where your friends use the host's Tailscale IP). The game
does not do NAT punching itself.

## Meet the city

Ten residents, each with their own patch of downtown:

| Who | Where |
|-----|-------|
| Marge Holloway, baker | Marge's Bakery, north-west |
| Officer Dana Brooks | outside the police station |
| Theo Park, barista | Bean There Coffee |
| Ms. Adaeze Obi, librarian | the library steps |
| Hal Jensen, hardware man | Jensen Hardware |
| Gus Romano, hot-dog vendor | the cart, dead center of the plaza |
| Ray Okafor, taxi driver | idling by his cab, east of the plaza |
| Yuki Tanaka, tourist | photographing the fountain |
| Benny "Strings" Malone, busker | the park's street corner |
| Mr. Albert Whitfield, retired teacher | the park bench |

They know each other — ask Gus about the squeaky cart wheel and someone at
the hardware store may have opinions.

## Configuration

- `config/llm.cfg` — model, host/port, temperature, `keep_alive` (latency).
  Any model you have pulled in Ollama works; smaller = snappier.
- `config/keybindings.cfg` — key bindings (also editable in-game).
- `personas/*.persona` — the characters themselves. Edit freely; the file
  format is documented in [docs/DEVELOPER.md](docs/DEVELOPER.md).

## Development

Architecture, headless test workflow, and the latency playbook live in
[docs/DEVELOPER.md](docs/DEVELOPER.md). Short version:

```sh
make -C tests test      # full offline unit-test suite, no graphics libs required
```

I have a complete evidence-backed picture. Here is my inventory.

---

# Atmosphere & Narrative Texture Audit — LLM-NPC Town Game

## (1) Authored or assembled? — Authored, densely, but only in two layers: the persona text and one hand-laid map function. Everything else is bare.

**Strong evidence of hand-authoring:**
- The entire city is one hand-written function, `City::makeDowntown()` at `src/core/City.cpp:18-76`. Not procedural — every building, prop, and car is a literal AABB with an explicit comment explaining the design intent: "3x3 city blocks on a 64-unit pitch... The center block is an open plaza; the north-east block is a park" (`City.cpp:19-22`).
- Named landmarks with sign text are authored individually: `{"bakery", "Marge's Bakery", ...}`, `{"police", "City Police Station", ...}`, `{"coffee", "Bean There Coffee", ...}`, `{"library", "City Library", ...}`, `{"hardware", "Jensen Hardware", ...}`, `{"cart", "Gus's Hot Dogs", ...}` (`City.cpp:27-34`).
- Props placed with narrative reasoning in comments: parked cars "curbside on the two Z-running streets... Spots avoid the zebra crossings... shop doors, and every persona's home position. The police car parks beside its station block." (`City.cpp:52-60`); "Alley props: dumpster + trash between the SW apartments" (`City.cpp:63-66`).

**Evidence of "assembled":**
- Filler buildings are anonymous grid density: `apt_a`, `apt_b`, `office_a`, `apts_c`, `tower` — all with empty name strings, commented "Unnamed filler so every block reads as a dense city" (`City.cpp:68-73`).
- Building facades are tinted by a hash, not by identity: `tint = 120 + (b.facadeKind * 37) % 90` (`src/app/RaylibRenderer.cpp:242-243`).
- The authored sign text (`Building.name`, documented as "sign / label text" at `City.hpp:16-17`) is **never rendered in the 3D world.** I found no `DrawText3D`/billboard for building names anywhere in `RaylibRenderer.cpp`. The only in-world floating text is NPC nameplates (`main.cpp:153-160`) and combat/action barks. So "Marge's Bakery" exists as data but a player never sees a bakery sign.

## (2) Named, characterized NPCs — exactly 10, each richly written (~800-1060 bytes)

The roster is fixed at ten, enforced by a test: `REQUIRE(roster.size() == 10)` (`tests/test_persona_roster.cpp:22`). One NPC per `.persona` file, loaded at `src/app/main.cpp:209-215`.

The ten, all with full name + role + traits + speaking style + knowledge boundary + placement + free-form directives:
- **Marge Holloway**, baker (`baker.persona`) — warm, gossipy, motherly; smells Bean There Coffee "two blocks over when the wind is right."
- **Officer Dana Brooks**, beat cop (`cop.persona`) — dry-humored, `armed = true`, buys rye "every Friday."
- **Theo Park**, barista (`barista.persona`) — aspiring screenwriter writing "a screenplay about a barista who solves crimes."
- **Ms. Adaeze Obi**, librarian (`librarian.persona`) — recommends fictional-but-plausible books, "Nothing about the internet; the card catalogue is authority enough."
- **Hal Jensen**, hardware owner (`hardware.persona`) — "measure twice," fixed the fountain pump "Twice."
- **Gus Romano**, hot-dog vendor (`hotdog.persona`) — "Ketchup on a dog is a crime."
- **Ray Okafor**, taxi driver (`taxi.persona`) — calls everyone "boss," offers "rides nobody needs."
- **Yuki Tanaka**, tourist (`tourist.persona`) — "photographed the fountain forty times," map upside down.
- **Benny "Strings" Malone**, busker (`musician.persona`) — "the fountain in the plaza hums in B-flat."
- **Mr. Albert Whitfield**, retired teacher (`teacher.persona`) — starts stories "back in my day," taught half the shopkeepers.

**Depth per NPC is high and interconnected.** The `knowledge` fields deliberately cross-reference each other, forming a social web authored entirely in text:
- Marge knows "Officer Brooks buys rye every Friday and that Theo at Bean There Coffee burns his espresso" (`baker.persona`).
- Theo disputes exactly that: "Marge across town says he burns his espresso (he disputes this)" (`barista.persona`).
- The squeaky-cart feud: Gus's cart "squeaks because Gus won't buy the right bearing" (`hardware.persona`) / "Hal at the hardware store keeps nagging about a squeaky wheel bearing" (`hotdog.persona`).
- Benny gets "free espresso" from Theo (`musician.persona`); Ray gets ticketed by Brooks (`taxi.persona`); Whitfield taught Marge ("excellent penmanship"), Theo ("never finished an essay"), Brooks ("hall monitor, naturally") (`teacher.persona`).

Four NPCs have **daily schedules** (position + activity by hour): baker, barista, musician, teacher (e.g. `barista.persona`: `schedule = 15-17, 60, 70, coffee break in the park`). Schedule format defined at `src/core/Schedule.hpp:11-18`, driven by one shared world clock. The other six are static.

Structured fields per persona: `name, role, traits, style, knowledge, spot, position, facing`, optional `armed`/`police`, optional `schedule` lines, and free-form directives after `---` (parser at `src/core/PersonaLoader.hpp:33-46`; struct at `src/core/Persona.hpp:11-19`).

There is also a **dynamic gossip layer**, but it ships empty. `factsKnownBy` is queried per NPC (`main.cpp:266`) and facts propagate on a seeded timer (`gossipRng(20260706u)`, `main.cpp:516`), but I found **no pre-seeded authored facts** — the fact store starts blank and fills only from player conversations (`src/core/Gossip.cpp:69-77`). All the authored cross-character texture lives in the static `knowledge` strings, not the runtime fact bus.

## (3) Sense of place — Local identity is strong in TEXT, near-absent in the RENDERED world.

- **In persona text:** vivid and specific. Directions are given by smell and shop, not street names ("give them in terms of shops and smells" — `baker.persona`); relative geography is consistent across files (bakery SW corner, police across the street east, coffee SE block by the office tower, library W steps facing plaza, hardware E block facing plaza, plaza fountain center, park NE corner). This is a coherent, walkable mental map.
- **In the world map:** the plaza and park are real spatial zones (`City.cpp:19-22`, `RaylibRenderer.cpp:210-213` special-cases plaza/park ground tint), and a hand-composed fountain is drawn from primitives (`RaylibRenderer.cpp:227-231`). But the **town has no name** — grep across personas/README/docs found no proper noun for the city; it is only ever "downtown"/"the city." No era or setting fiction is stated anywhere (README `README.md:1-9` frames premise only as "a small first-person 3D city where every inhabitant is a live LLM character"). No in-world signage renders (see §1). So place-identity is authored for the LLM's mouth, not for the player's eyes.

## (4) Ambient / environmental detail — what exists vs. absent

**Exists (static props with real colliders, authored in `City.cpp`):**
- 4 traffic lights at block corners (`City.cpp:42-45`)
- 4 bushes in the park (`City.cpp:46-49`)
- 5 parked cars incl. a police car by the station (`City.cpp:56-60`)
- 2 dumpster/trash clusters in alleys (`City.cpp:64-66`)
- Fountain, bench, hot-dog cart, idle taxi (`City.cpp:34-37`)
- Day/night cycle: sky color + brightness curves over a 24h clock, four bands with dawn/dusk blends (`src/core/DayNight.hpp:8-13, 24-26`). This is the single largest source of ambient atmosphere.

**Absent entirely:**
- **No pedestrians, no crowds.** Grep for `pedestrian|crowd` returns zero. The only movers are the 10 named NPCs; there are no anonymous background people.
- **No moving traffic.** The 5 cars are static collider props (`City.cpp:56-60`); the taxi is "idling"/parked. Traffic lights don't cycle (no state logic — they're just `facadeKind 11` obstacles).
- **No audio of any kind.** No `InitAudioDevice`, `LoadSound`, `LoadMusicStream`, or any `.wav/.ogg/.mp3` asset anywhere in `src/`. The word "audio" appears only in a comment about future routing (`src/core/CombatEvents.hpp:9`). No music, no ambience, no footsteps, no fountain sound (despite Benny's line about it humming in B-flat).
- **No in-world text/signage** beyond floating NPC nameplates and combat barks (§1).
- **Unused atmosphere assets on disk:** `streetlight.bin` and `firehydrant.bin` exist under `assets/models/city/` but are **not placed** in `City.cpp` (grep found neither id in the map), so they never appear.

---

**Bottom line:** The narrative texture is almost entirely carried by ~9 KB of hand-written persona prose — ten deeply characterized, socially interlinked residents with consistent geography, feuds, and history. The spatial world is genuinely hand-authored (not procedural) but thin on visible detail: no town name, no rendered signs, no crowds, no moving traffic, and no sound at all. A player *reading* the NPCs feels a lived-in town; a player *looking at and listening to* the world sees a quiet, static asset grid with a nice day/night sky.
